name: Rattlesnake oil

lead: Rattlesnake oil is fat rendered from rattlesnakes, used as a rub for rheumatism and skin diseases. It was favoured in nineteenth-century America and sold in bottled liniments; the appearance angle is the claim that it soothed skin disease and joint pain when rubbed on.

Its medical effectiveness was never thoroughly tested. In about 1916 the US Bureau of Chemistry analysed Clark Stanley's Snake Oil Liniment and reported mineral oil, about 1% fatty oil, capsaicin, turpentine and camphor.

paras: Historically it was applied topically as a liniment, rubbed into painful joints or affected skin. It was sold at medicine shows and in bottled form.

Products sold under the name varied and could contain ingredients such as turpentine and camphor. Regulators prosecuted a leading seller for misbranding, and the phrase 'snake oil' now describes dubious remedies.

chain: Oil or liniment rubbed onto skin
Claimed relief of rheumatism and skin disease
angle.text: Users applied it as a rub for skin disease and sore joints. The skin benefit is a traditional claim and has not been tested.

lead: Rattlesnake oil is a folk remedy made from the fat of American pit vipers, used as a liniment for rheumatism and skin diseases. It followed earlier European use of viper oil for many ailments in the eighteenth century.[1]
In an appearance context, its claimed benefit was on skin conditions when rubbed on. Its medical effectiveness was never thoroughly tested.[1]
Its name became widely known through Clark Stanley, the 'Rattlesnake King', whose product the Bureau of Chemistry tested around 1916.[1]

paras: Eighteenth-century Europeans, especially in Britain, recommended viper oil, and rattlesnake oil later became the favoured version in America.[1] After the Civil War, medicine shows combined entertainment with selling remedies, some of which contained alcohol or narcotics.[1]

Much of the 'snake oil' sold in the UK and US probably contained no snake, and may have been modified mineral oil with herbs.[1] A forum post on T Nation recalls the nineteenth-century travelling salesman and his shill in the crowd, drawing on a Scientific American piece about omega-3 supplements.[2]

The Bureau of Chemistry, a forerunner of the FDA, tested Stanley's liniment around 1916 and reported mineral oil, about 1% fatty oil assumed to be tallow, capsaicin, turpentine and camphor. He was prosecuted in federal court in Rhode Island for misbranding and for claiming it cured sciatica, sore throat and aches; he pleaded no contest and was fined $20.[1]
The Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906 and the later FDA are credited with ending the patent medicine industry in the US.[1]

timeline.event: Pure Food and Drug Act passes in the US.[1]
Bureau of Chemistry tests Clark Stanley's Snake Oil Liniment; he is fined.[1]
